findings.claim: Three threads make the connection explicit.
findings.evidence: The paragraph lists five: Ch 2, Ch 3, Ch 9, Ch 11-12, Ch 14.
findings.fix: correct: Five threads make the connection explicit.

findings.claim: The text explicitly frames against using arbitration clauses "as a way to keep wrongdoings 'quiet' or to limit consumers' abilities to obtain rightful retribution."
findings.evidence: Words match source 1289-1290 and deep 110/939.
findings.fix: re-mark: [V]

findings.claim: consequentialist reasoning is structurally appropriate but the deontological frame catches actions that "everyone doing them would harm."
findings.failure_mode: paraphrase in quotation marks; evaluative claim not in source
findings.evidence: Source 1154-1156: 'one's action should be considered in light of what would happen if everyone were to engage in the same action.' 'everyone doing them would harm' is not source text. Deep 86-88 and source take no position that consequentialism is 'structurally appropriate' for stakeholder decisions; they note only that 100% deontology is very difficult in dispute resolution.
findings.fix: correct: Stakeholder decisions often weigh impacts on parties without voice; the deontological frame adds Kant's test of whether the action would be acceptable if everyone did it (Ch 2.2, "Ethical Issues").

findings.claim: Employers may be liable for non-employee harassment if they fail to remedy.
findings.failure_mode: in source but not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 621-628 omits it. Source 5152-5154: 'In some limited circumstances, employers may also be liable for harassment of employees by non-employees, e.g., customers. The employer is liable if it does nothing to prevent and remedy harassment targeted at one of its employees.'
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 628: 'In some limited circumstances, employers may also be liable for harassment of employees by non-employees, e.g., customers' [V] (Ch 9.3).

findings.claim: requires ... statements of ownership for corporate insiders owning more than 10%
findings.failure_mode: in source but not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 842 defines corporate insiders (>10%) but carries no filing duty. Source 7016-7017: 'Corporate insiders must file a statement of ownership with the SEC to be in compliance'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 842: 'Corporate insiders must file a statement of ownership with the SEC to be in compliance' [V] (Ch 14.1, "Insider Transactions").

findings.claim: doctrine of sovereign immunity (qualified post-1976)
findings.evidence: Deep 782: 'The US adapted to qualified immunity in 1952; the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976 allows US governance of foreign-state lawsuits' when immunity is waived or the activity causes a direct US effect.
findings.fix: correct: doctrine of sovereign immunity (qualified in the US from 1952; codified in the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976)

findings.claim: Apply Thomas-Kilmann mode | ... competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, yielding?
findings.evidence: Business Law's TKI label is 'forcing' (deep 55); 'competing' is OB's label (OB deep 444). The distillation uses 'forcing' everywhere else.
findings.fix: correct: forcing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, yielding

findings.claim: Could the harm have been reasonably foreseen? This drives both tort liability and ethical responsibility.
findings.failure_mode: extends a negligence concept to ethics without source support
findings.evidence: Deep 334-336: foreseeability is the negligence test (Ch 6.1). The source does not tie foreseeability to ethical responsibility.
findings.fix: correct: Could the harm have been reasonably foreseen? Foreseeability drives negligence liability (Ch 6.1).

findings.claim: Apply procedural justice | Even when distributive outcomes disappoint, fair process sustains commitment.
findings.evidence: 'Procedural justice' does not occur in the Business Law source or deep. It is carried by openstax-organizational-behavior-deep 239 (Ch 7.4, organisational justice).
findings.fix: correct: Apply procedural justice | Are we applying a fair process regardless of which way the outcome goes? (see OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 7.4 on procedural justice)

findings.claim: Arbitration (binding or non-binding; with subject-matter expert via baseball arbitration)?
findings.failure_mode: in source but not in deep; conflates two stipulations
findings.evidence: Deep 114 frames baseball arbitration as a fix for arbitrators lacking subject-matter expertise and omits the expert stipulation. Source 1320-1323: the owner 'could write a lease agreement that stipulates that the parties use binding baseball arbitration and use subject matter experts as arbitrators'. Baseball arbitration and expert arbitrators are two separate stipulations.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 114: the lease can stipulate 'binding baseball arbitration and use subject matter experts as arbitrators' [V] (Ch 2.3, "Arbitration Procedures"). Then correct: Arbitration (binding or non-binding; with subject-matter-expert arbitrators, or baseball arbitration)?

findings.claim: Diagnosis: the source is explicit that this damages brand more than it builds it.
findings.evidence: Deep 181: 'Consumers will quickly pick up on this tactic, and it can damage the brand.' No comparison with brand-building.
findings.fix: correct: Diagnosis: the source is explicit that consumers "will quickly pick up on this tactic, and it can damage the brand" [V] (Ch 3.2).

findings.claim: Diagnosis: Rule 10b-5 violation potential. Follow-up: pre-arrange via Rule 10b5-1 plan well in advance, with predetermined dates and amounts.
findings.failure_mode: Rule 10b-5 not in deep; follow-up drops the good-faith-beforehand condition
findings.evidence: Rule 10b-5 is in source 6956-6958 but not in deep 832. Source 6991-6993: a 10b5-1 plan must be 'arranged in good faith beforehand'; deep 838 omits 'in good faith'. An insider already holding the information cannot fix it by setting up a plan now.
findings.fix: correct: Follow-up: do not trade on the information; future trades can use a Rule 10b5-1 plan arranged in good faith beforehand, with predetermined dates and pre-set amounts (Ch 14.1). Also cycle-to-deep: add Rule 10b-5 and 'arranged in good faith beforehand' to deep 832/838.

findings.claim: This worked example illustrates ... the deontological frame on forced-arbitration clauses, CSR alignment with operational reality, and procedural justice across multiple stakeholder groups.
findings.failure_mode: concepts named as illustrated that the example and source do not carry
findings.evidence: The example's arbitration decision (line 158) rests on reputational cost, a consequentialist reason, not a deontological one; the example has no CSR step; 'procedural justice' is not in the Business Law source or deep.
findings.fix: correct: This worked example illustrates stakeholder mapping by legal-relationship type, relational-versus-outcome framing, ADR-tier selection, and disparate-impact analysis.

findings.claim: The WARN Act notice obligation, NLRA collective-bargaining requirement, FTC pre-merger notification, Title VII disparate-impact analysis, and Thomas-Kilmann conflict-mode vocabulary (Ch 2) are `[AP]`-marked passages in the deep ref.
findings.evidence: Deep 575, 578 (NLRA, WARN) and 698 (1976 Clayton amendment) carry no marker; WARN's 60 days is [V] in the key-stats table (883); Title VII's [AP] (616) covers the ban and threshold, not the disparate-impact bullet (619); TKI is [V, BT] (53).
findings.fix: correct: These passages are carried in the deep ref's Ch 2, Ch 9 and Ch 11 sections (TKI as [V, BT]; the WARN 60-day notice as [V]); the rest are unmarked paraphrase.

findings.claim: Reputational and referral costs typically exceed near-term gains.
findings.evidence: Deep 55: forcing 'often undermines the party's long-term success'; source 966-968 illustrates with lost reviews and referrals. No claim that costs 'typically exceed' gains.
findings.fix: correct: Forcing "often undermines the party's long-term success" [V] (Ch 2.1), for example through negative reviews and lost referrals.

findings.claim: Ignoring the procedural-justice dimension of employment decisions. Even fair distributive outcomes can produce litigation if the process feels unfair.
findings.evidence: No procedural-justice content in Business Law deep or source; OB deep 239 (Ch 7.4) carries procedural justice but makes no litigation claim.
findings.fix: strip

findings.claim: Voluntary compliance through consent orders typically produces better long-term outcomes than litigation.
findings.evidence: Deep 737-741 lists consent order as one FTC recourse option, with no outcome comparison.
findings.fix: correct: Treating regulators as adversaries rather than as stakeholders. The FTC's options include voluntary compliance through a consent order before administrative complaints or federal litigation (Ch 12.2).

findings.claim: Hiding material nonpublic information rather than disclosing on time. The 4-business-day Form 8-K window, the 10-day Schedule 13D window, and the 40-day proxy notice window each carry consequences for missing.
findings.failure_mode: 13D mis-framed as event disclosure; consequences not in source
findings.evidence: Deep 842: Schedule 13D is a >5% beneficial-ownership filing. Figures match deep 842-851. Neither deep nor source states consequences for missing the 8-K, 13D or proxy windows (source 7021-7022 speaks only of insider-reporting compliance).
findings.fix: correct: Missing disclosure windows. Form 8-K events within four business days, Schedule 13D within 10 days of crossing 5% ownership, proxy notice at least 40 days before the meeting (Ch 14.1).

findings.claim: Stakeholder theory (Freeman, not in source) | The OpenStax text never cites Freeman ...

findings.fix: correct: openstax-principles-management (Ch 5.6, Freeman) | Principles of Management carries stakeholder theory and eight stakeholder-analysis questions; Business Law supplies the legal architecture (Title VII, ADA, FTC, NLRA, securities law) behind each stakeholder's claims. Business Law does not cite Freeman.

findings.claim: consumers have collective expert and economic power
findings.failure_mode: power base not in French and Raven's five
findings.evidence: OB deep 360-366 (Ch 12.3): reward, coercive, referent, expert, legitimate. 'Economic power' is not one of the five.
findings.fix: correct: regulators have legitimate power, unions have collective coercive power, consumers have collective reward power (their purchasing)

findings.claim: Procedural justice | The Title VII three-step burden shifting and the FMLA / ADA / FCRA process requirements all express procedural-justice principles in legal form.
findings.failure_mode: statute not in source; framing not in either deep
findings.evidence: FCRA does not occur in the source. Business Law deep does not frame Title VII, FMLA or ADA as procedural justice. The corpus holds procedural justice in openstax-organizational-behavior-deep 239 (Ch 7.4).
findings.fix: correct: openstax-organizational-behavior (Ch 7.4) | OB distinguishes distributive from procedural justice (seniority-based layoffs are perceived as more procedurally just); pair with Business Law's Title VII seniority defence (Ch 9.3) when structuring layoffs.

findings.claim: Coase / transaction-cost economics (not in source)

findings.claim: the text favours balanced ethical analysis (Ch 2.2)

findings.claim: The deep reference ... uses [V], [AP], [AR], [AE], and [BT] markers ... The forced-arbitration critique and CSR-as-marketing critique are [AR] (author argument).
findings.evidence: The deep contains zero [AR] markers. The CSR-as-marketing sentence is [V] (deep 181); the forced-arbitration normative sentence is unmarked verbatim (deep 110). The count of 22 exact [BT] markers checks out.
findings.fix: correct: The deep reference uses [V], [AP], [AE] and [BT] markers (22 standalone [BT]). The CSR-as-marketing critique is [V]; the forced-arbitration critique is the author's words, quoted verbatim.

findings.claim: OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 14 uses the same vocabulary for conflict resolution.
findings.evidence: OB deep 442-448 labels two of the five modes differently: competing (Business Law: forcing) and accommodating (Business Law: yielding); OB frames them on assertiveness x cooperativeness.
findings.fix: correct: OpenStax Organizational Behavior Ch 14 uses the same five-mode model under partly different labels (competing for forcing, accommodating for yielding).

notes: Cleanest of the three: Key Concepts are largely faithful and all [V] quotes match the converted source. Drift clusters in the integration table (three rows point outside the corpus or to concepts the corpus holds elsewhere; Habermas and FCRA absent entirely) and in the citation-integrity tail (statutes labelled [BT], [AR] claimed where the deep has none). Procedural justice is threaded through the file (E009, E013, E016, E022) without Business Law support. Worked example carries no verbatim blockquote and says so (line 162); not graded. The worked-example scenario outcome (six months, no lawsuits) is presented as hypothetical, not as a source finding.
